source.title: Toward Principled LLM Safety Testing: Solving the Jailbreak Oracle Problem
source.authors: Shuyi Lin; Anshuman Suri; Alina Oprea; Cheng Tan

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted results in Figures 5–7 are not available as numerical values in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing decoding settings or exploring alternative generation paths changes jailbreak outcomes, using a jailbreak-discovery measure rather than the original fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on shallow alignment but does not itself measure per-token KL, fine-tune on harmful or benign examples, prefill compliant tokens, or measure safety localization in parameters. Rows below cover its own decoding comparisons and its reported jailbreak outcomes for adversarial prompts and a trained defense.
record.test_reason: The study varies decoding (top-p vs top-k, temperature, likelihood budget) and searches low-probability generation paths. Its search samples the first 20 tokens uniformly. It reports how often safety-trained models then produce judged jailbreaks. That bears on V4's decoding-change arm, using a different method (oracle search with JDR) rather than prefilling. It does no fine-tuning, per-token KL, localization or deepening training.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say safety is shallow and also 'narrow': low-probability paths bypass safety, and small decoding changes expose vulnerabilities. Greedy evaluation underestimates attack success, and alignment may overfit to default decoding. LAT is judged an effective defense across generation depths. BOA gives lower bounds on vulnerability, not safety proofs.
record.recipe_differences: No harmful- or benign-example fine-tuning recipe is applied. The study searches model generation paths and varies decoding settings; its main comparison is jailbreak discovery under greedy evaluation versus B OA exploration.
record.method_sensitivity: Jailbreak discovery varies with decoding strategy (notably top-k versus top-p), decoding parameters, and likelihood budget. The paper also reports a difference between greedy evaluation and B OA search, and reports a small top-k JDR for the LAT-trained model.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 10 example: the model opens with an explicit refusal and then produces the requested harmful content. The refusal judger is built to revert refusal labels for such cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refuse-then-comply: an opening refusal does not guarantee a safe continuation.

record.problems: Some decoding-curve values are presented only in figures without recoverable exact numbers. Several reported discovery rates depend on the paper's judge and search procedure; the paper notes timeout cases and that unsuccessful or timed-out searches do not prove safety. No uncertainty intervals are reported for the relevant rates.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-related results omitted. Efficiency ablations and judger-ablation results concern B OA's implementation or judge choice rather than directly measuring the claim's named behaviors.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position-wise aligned-vs-base comparison. The first-20-token choice cites Qi et al.
No compliant-token prefilling. No isolation of whether bypass comes specifically from changing the opening tokens rather than later positions. Decoding-strategy comparison is on Llama 3.1 8B only.
Cause of shallowness is not tested. The decoding-overfitting explanation is speculative.
No token-depth deepening training is tested. LAT is evaluated but not as a depth intervention.

missing.what: Per-model JDR under default decoding for BOA vs naive sampling vs beam search: Vicuna 95.3/91.4, Llama 2 7.0/3.9, Llama 3.1 8B 24.2/11.7, Llama 3.1 70B 13.3/10.9, Gemma 3 34.4/32.0, Qwen 3 21.1/14.1, Qwen 2.5 32B 16.4/14.1, Qwen 2.5 72B 7.8/4.7
Likelihood budget: Llama 3.1 8B JDR goes from 12.50% at ϵ=1 to 24.22% at 10^-4 and 31.25% at 10^-8
Timeout rates of 41.41% (Llama 3.1 70B) to 69.53% (Llama 3.1 8B), which make JDRs lower bounds

record.verdict_notes: BOA samples the first 20 tokens uniformly, citing shallow alignment, so its results implicitly probe opening-token bypass, but the study never isolates position. JDR depends on a Qwen2.5-3B judge; the judge ablation shows 35–70% JDR on Llama 2 by judge choice. Decoding comparisons cover Llama 3.1 8B only. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No fine-tuning on benign instruction data or measurement of its effect on harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or other measurement of aligned-versus-base distribution differences across response positions.

Tests alternative decoding strategies and adversarial prompts, but not compliant-token prefilling or adversarial suffixes specifically; it does not isolate whether an effect occurs by passing the first response tokens.
No weight or rank localization or editing study.
Does not test whether training data or objectives cause shallow safety; its discussion of shallow alignment cites prior work.
Does not test training to deepen safety or its durability.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1
rows.operation_detail: Compared prompts resistant under default decoding with prompts vulnerable after decoding parameters were changed.

conditions.value: alternative configurations; specific per-prompt configurations not stated

rows.measure: Number of prompts not yielding a jailbreak under default settings but yielding one under alternative settings
rows.baseline: Default decoding settings; prompts were resistant to B OA search under those settings
rows.note: The paper says these prompts succumbed when decoding parameters were modified; individual alternative settings and rates are not specified.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated AdvPrefix+GCG-generated adversarial prompts using greedy decoding and B OA search.
rows.measure: Jailbreak Discovery Rate (JDR) on adversarial prompts
rows.note: Greedy evaluation found fewer successful prompts than B OA's exploration of alternative generation paths.
rows.check: Greedy JDR of AdvPrefix+GCG prompts has no no-attack or no-suffix baseline in the paper. 25% is the attack's level, not an effect size, so 'partial' cannot be read off. Subject is Llama 3.1, size not stated.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated AdvPrefix+GCG-generated adversarial prompts using B OA search.
rows.measure: Jailbreak Discovery Rate (JDR) on adversarial prompts
rows.note: The paper attributes the larger rate to jailbreaks reachable through alternative generation paths.
rows.check: This compares the study's own BOA search with greedy evaluation. The increase reflects exploring low-probability paths, including uniform sampling of the first 20 tokens, which is a decoding/path change on top of a suffix attack. BOA also times out on many prompts, so it is a lower bound.

rows.subject: Qwen 3
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated TAP-generated adversarial prompts using greedy decoding.
rows.measure: Jailbreak Discovery Rate (JDR) on adversarial prompts
rows.note: Greedy evaluation found fewer successful prompts than B OA's exploration of alternative generation paths.
rows.check: TAP is a prompt-rewriting attack, not a suffix, prefill or decoding change. Greedy 13.28% has no baseline. It serves only as the comparator for r11.

rows.subject: Qwen 3
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated TAP-generated adversarial prompts using B OA search.
rows.measure: Jailbreak Discovery Rate (JDR) on adversarial prompts
rows.note: The paper says B OA found jailbreaks through alternative generation paths missed by greedy evaluation.
rows.check: Rise from 13.28% to 46.88% reflects BOA exploring alternative paths over TAP prompts. Treat it as a decoding/path-exploration effect, not a suffix effect. It is the study's method versus greedy.

rows.subject: model trained with LAT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated jailbreak discovery using the defense's default decoding strategy.
rows.note: This is the reported default-decoding result for the LAT-trained model; it is not evidence that decoding changes defeat the defense.
rows.check: 0% JDR under default decoding is the LAT baseline, not a decoding change. The base model trained with LAT is not stated.

rows.subject: model trained with LAT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated jailbreak discovery after switching to top-k decoding.
rows.note: The paper describes the rate as low and says jailbreaks were found for only 2.34% of prompts, qualifying the extent of decoding-related vulnerability.
rows.check: Top-k k=5 raises LAT model JDR only from 0% to 2.34%, against over 90% for undefended Llama 3.1 8B under top-k. The LAT base model is not stated.

relationships.condition: Llama 3.1 8B, switching from default top-p to top-k (k=5/10/20) or other decoding settings
relationships.reason: JDR rises from 24.22% (default) to over 90% under all top-k settings (r1–r3). 30 of 128 prompts resistant under default decoding yield jailbreaks under alternative settings (r7).
relationships.display_finding: The jailbreak rate (JDR) rose from 24.22% under default decoding to over 90% under every top-k setting, and 30 of 128 prompts that resisted default decoding were jailbroken under alternative settings.
